strengths: Novel and well-motivated intermediate representation: multi-modal (RGB+semantic+geometric) panoramic renderings that bridge 2D VLMs and 3D scenes, avoiding both fully training-from-scratch 3D encoders and unreliable zero-shot view selection used in prior VLM-agent approaches.

The full pipeline is coherently engineered: structure-aware camera placement with an interpretable scoring function (ray coverage, distance-to-surface, distance-to-trajectory), a lightweight zero-initialized adapter that injects geometric/semantic cues into selected ViT layers without disturbing pretrained VLM behavior, and a visibility-aware multi-view fusion/lifting procedure.
Strong and consistent empirical results: state-of-the-art or near state-of-the-art on ScanRefer and Nr3D under both single-dataset and mixed-dataset training regimes, and competitive results on Sr3D.

Thorough and informative ablations covering input modalities/training objectives (Table 5), camera placement strategy components (Table 6, Fig. 7-8), number of cameras and test-time rotations (Fig. 7, 9), mesh vs. 3DGS scene representation (Table 7, Fig. 10), and adapter initialization strategy — these substantiate the design choices rather than simply reporting final numbers.

Generalization experiments are a highlight: cross-dataset evaluation on unseen ARKitScenes/3RScan scenes and robustness to four types of LLM-generated text perturbations (rephrasing, affordance-based, affordance without target noun, masked target name) show the method degrades much less than competing baselines, supporting the core claim that panoramic 2D-VLM grounding generalizes better than dataset-specific 3D encoders.

The panorama-vs-pinhole comparison (Table 4) is a useful and non-trivial experiment demonstrating that panoramic context specifically helps for queries mentioning multiple objects, going beyond a simple existence proof of the design choice.

Good reproducibility effort: detailed hyperparameters, prompt templates, rendering configuration, and training convergence curves are provided in the supplementary material; runtime is also reported (3.3s/query).
weaknesses: Results are not uniformly best across all settings — on Sr3D the method trails VGMamba/UniVLG, and on the cross-dataset ScanNetV2/ARKitScenes/3RScan evaluation (Table 2) PanoGrounder underperforms several specialized baselines on some subsets (e.g., ScanRefer 'unique' vs MCLN, ARKitScenes 'unique' is close to BUTD-DETR); the paper's narrative emphasizes wins but could more candidly characterize where it is not the top performer.

The backbone is a large pretrained VLM (CogVLM-17B) fine-tuned with LoRA; the paper does not report parameter counts, training compute, or inference cost comparisons against the (typically much smaller) supervised 3DVG baselines it compares against, making it hard to judge whether gains are partly attributable to sheer backbone scale rather than the proposed architecture.

The 3D lifting pipeline depends on an auxiliary segmentation model (SAM) for mask-to-3D lifting and on a heuristic best-view selection via cross-view IoU consistency; failure modes of this dependency (e.g., SAM mask errors, degenerate best-view selection in highly occluded scenes) are not analyzed.

The camera placement scoring function (Eq. 1) and its hyperparameters (radius, grid spacing, coverage threshold) are hand-tuned heuristics; while ablated, there is limited theoretical or systematic justification for the specific 90% coverage threshold or the multiplicative combination of the three factors.

Limitations discussion is brief and largely forward-looking (no-target/multi-target queries, multi-task extension) without deeper analysis of current failure cases beyond a few qualitative examples in the appendix; a more quantitative error analysis (e.g., failure rate breakdown by scene clutter, occlusion, or object size) would strengthen the soundness claims.

The method assumes a renderable 3D scene representation (mesh or 3DGS) is available at test time, which is reasonable for the benchmarks used but constrains applicability compared to methods operating directly on raw point clouds; this practical constraint is not explicitly discussed as a limitation.

strengths: The core idea of using 360° panoramic renderings (RGB + geometry + semantic features) as an explicit 2D-3D intermediate interface for pretrained VLMs is a reasonable and relatively fresh angle on connecting 2D vision-language reasoning to 3D grounding, avoiding both the viewpoint-selection brittleness of zero-shot multi-turn VLM agents and the heavy architectural surgery of fully fine-tuned 3D-VLM hybrids.

The pipeline is thoughtfully engineered: structure-aware camera placement with an interpretable scoring function (ray coverage, distance-to-surface, distance-to-trajectory), a lightweight zero-initialized adapter for injecting geometric/semantic cues into VLM ViT layers, and a visibility-aware multi-view fusion/lifting scheme for going from 2D boxes back to a 3D box.

The experimental section is broad: results on ScanRefer and Nr3D/Sr3D, cross-dataset generalization to ARKitScenes/3RScan, text-robustness evaluation under LLM-generated paraphrases/affordance queries/masking, panorama-vs-pinhole comparisons, and a large ablation suite (modalities, losses, camera placement components, mesh vs. 3DGS, test-time augmentation, adapter initialization) in the supplementary.

Reported numbers are competitive to state-of-the-art on several splits (notably Nr3D and ScanRefer Multiple), and the qualitative figures plausibly illustrate the intended benefits of panoramic context (holistic relational cues, robustness to occlusion) versus a 3D-VisTA baseline.
The EMD-based numeric-aware loss and geometric QA auxiliary task are simple, well-motivated additions with supporting ablations showing incremental gains.
weaknesses: The claim of a 'simpler, more efficient' interface is not well supported by the actual pipeline complexity: it requires RANSAC floor estimation, greedy camera placement, rendering three separate panoramic modalities per viewpoint (RGB, depth, aggregated multi-view semantic feature field), a frozen DINOv2 encoder for semantic features, SAM-based mask-to-3D lifting, cross-view consistency scoring, and LoRA fine-tuning of a 17B VLM with several auxiliary losses/QA tasks — this is arguably more moving parts than some of the fine-tuning baselines it criticizes, undermining the 'minimal modifications around the VLM' framing.

The method is evaluated with only a single VLM backbone (CogVLM-17B); no ablation demonstrates that the panorama-as-interface idea transfers to other VLMs, which is important for a paper whose central claim is a general recipe for 'VLM-based 3D visual grounding.'

The benchmark leadership claims are inconsistent with the actual tables: on Sr3D the method is not top-1 (VGMamba and UniVLG report higher Overall), and in the cross-dataset ScanNetV2/ARKitScenes/3RScan table the proposed method is not best on several Unique/Multiple subsets (e.g., ScanRefer Unique 91.7 vs. 93.4/92.5 for MCLN/BUTD-DETR), so 'state-of-the-art' language is somewhat overstated relative to the mixed evidence.

The method still requires supervised fine-tuning on ScanRefer/Referit3D-style annotations (with LoRA), so it is not zero-shot; the paper's framing sometimes implies stronger generalization/zero-shot-like behavior than what is actually demonstrated, and no direct head-to-head comparison against true zero-shot VLM-agent baselines (e.g., VLM-Grounder, SeeGround) is provided on the same benchmarks.

Robustness table 3 shows the proposed model is not uniformly superior to baselines (e.g., PQ3D scores higher on the original and rephrased queries), with the model's advantage concentrated specifically in the harder Aff.†/Mask settings; this nuance somewhat tempers the 'robust across diverse textual perturbations' claim.

Reliance on ground-truth object segmentation/instance masks for several robustness and cross-dataset evaluations (Table 2, 3) makes those comparisons partially decoupled from a fully end-to-end, real-world deployment setting, and this dependency is not clearly flagged as a limitation in the main text.

No quantitative failure-case analysis or error breakdown is provided (only qualitative success/some failure figures), leaving open questions about systematic weaknesses (e.g., very small objects, camera-placement failures in cluttered/multi-room scenes) that a reviewer cannot verify are adequately addressed.

Reported per-query runtime (~3.3s, with 9.6 forward passes per query) plus offline camera-placement/rendering preprocessing raises practicality concerns for the embodied-AI applications motivated in the introduction, but this trade-off is not critically discussed relative to lighter single-view or lightweight fusion baselines.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated intermediate representation (multi-modal panoramic renderings) that bridges 2D pretrained VLMs and 3D scenes, avoiding the need to design 3D-specific decoding heads or view-selection heuristics used in prior zero-shot/fine-tuning approaches.

Comprehensive experimental validation: state-of-the-art or near state-of-the-art results on ScanRefer and Nr3D, competitive performance on Sr3D, plus dedicated scene-generalization (ARKitScenes/3RScan) and text-generalization (rephrasing/affordance/masking) experiments that convincingly demonstrate robustness beyond standard benchmark settings.

Thorough ablations covering camera placement strategy, number of cameras, input modalities (RGB/semantic/geometric), training objectives (EMD loss, geometric QA), scene representation (mesh vs 3DGS), adapter initialization, and test-time augmentation, giving good insight into what drives performance.

The structure-aware camera placement module is intuitively justified and empirically shown to need far fewer views (avg. 2.4/scene) than naive dense sampling to match/exceed random placement performance, which is a practically useful efficiency contribution.
Clear comparison against pinhole-view baselines (Table 4) isolates the benefit of panoramic FoV specifically for capturing multi-object relational context, strengthening the core design claim.
Reasonable transparency about limitations (no target / multi-target handling, single-task scope) and a runtime analysis in the supplementary material aids reproducibility assessment.
weaknesses: The method relies on multiple auxiliary off-the-shelf components (SAM for mask-to-3D lifting, DINOv2 features, RANSAC floor estimation, mesh/3DGS renderers) that add pipeline complexity and potential failure points not deeply analyzed for error propagation (e.g., how SAM segmentation errors affect final 3D box accuracy).

Performance on Sr3D and some ScanNet-based cross-dataset splits (ARKitScenes/3RScan Table 2) is sometimes below strong baselines (e.g., VGMamba on Sr3D, ViL3DRel/BUTD-DETR on ARKitScenes/3RScan unique splits), which somewhat tempers the 'state-of-the-art' claim and is not deeply discussed as a limitation.

The Earth Mover's Distance loss and digit-based coordinate regression choice, while empirically ablated, is a fairly specific engineering choice tied to the CogVLM output format; generality to other VLM backbones is not tested, limiting insight into whether gains are backbone-specific.

Only a single VLM backbone (CogVLM-17B) is used throughout; no ablation with alternative/more recent VLMs to show the panoramic representation's benefit transfers across different pretrained backbones.

The three-stage pipeline (camera placement, per-view VLM grounding, multi-view fusion) involves several hyperparameters (e.g., grid spacing, coverage threshold, IoU-based best-view selection) whose sensitivity is only partly explored, raising minor reproducibility concerns despite the supplementary detail provided.
Qualitative failure-case analysis is limited; the paper mostly shows successful examples (Fig. 11, 12) with less discussion of systematic failure modes beyond the 3DGS artifact discussion.

strengths: Well-motivated core idea: using panoramic renderings as a 2D-3D interface addresses a real limitation (narrow FoV) of prior pinhole-based VLM 3DVG methods, and the paper provides a clean ablation (Table 6) explicitly demonstrating the benefit of panoramas over pinhole views at matched conditions, including comparison against an oracle GT-target pinhole setting.

Strong and comprehensive experimental validation: state-of-the-art or near-SOTA results on ScanRefer and Nr3D/Sr3D under both single- and multi-dataset training regimes, plus zero-shot comparisons showing a much smaller backbone (CogVLM-17B) outperforming larger proprietary VLMs (GPT-4V, Qwen2-VL-72B).

Thorough generalization studies across unseen scene datasets (ARKitScenes, 3RScan) and systematic text perturbations (paraphrase, affordance-based, noun-masked), showing PanoGrounder's robustness advantage grows precisely in settings that require relational/semantic reasoning rather than lexical matching.

Extensive and thoughtful ablations in the supplementary material (camera placement scoring factors, adapter layer placement informed by probing analysis, zero-init adapters, EMD loss, geometric QA, TTA rotation count, mesh vs 3DGS representations, and even a real-world self-captured deployment with runtime/memory breakdown), which substantially strengthens reproducibility and mechanistic understanding of the method.

Good attribution and fair experimental protocol design (grouping single- vs multi-dataset baselines, re-running baselines for cross-dataset/text-robustness comparisons under matched GT-segmentation conditions), which increases confidence in the reported gains being genuine rather than artifacts of unfair comparison.
weaknesses: The pipeline has considerable complexity and many moving, hand-tuned parts (camera scoring formula with heuristic weighting, greedy 90% coverage threshold, SAM-based masking, cross-view IoU anchor selection, visibility filtering thresholds), which could hurt reproducibility and makes it harder to isolate which design choices are essential versus incidental; the main paper defers most of the load-bearing ablations to supplementary material.

The multi-stage lifting/fusion pipeline (VLM box -> SAM segmentation -> depth unprojection -> anchor selection -> outlier removal -> AABB fitting) introduces multiple potential failure/error-accumulation points that are not deeply analyzed for sensitivity (e.g., SAM failure modes, dependence on accurate depth/camera extrinsics), and the reported latency (3.3s/query with CogVLM-17B) may be a real deployment concern that is only partially mitigated by smaller backbones with a fairly large accuracy trade-off (61.0 vs 52.1 vs 45.6).

The method assumes availability of a renderable 3D reconstruction (mesh or 3DGS) computed offline; while a self-captured demo is provided, this offline dependency (COLMAP + 3DGS training taking well over two hours) somewhat limits the claimed 'minimal input requirement' narrative for real-time or dynamic-scene use cases, which is only partially acknowledged in limitations.

Some comparisons (e.g., zero-shot Table 2, cross-dataset Table 3) rely on re-running baselines by the authors themselves without releasing code/checkpoints (not verifiable from the manuscript), and the paper does not report variance/multiple seeds for the main results, making it hard to judge the statistical significance of relatively small margins in some subsets (e.g., Sr3D Hard, VD splits where PanoGrounder is not best).

strengths: The core idea of using panoramic renderings as an explicit 2D-3D interface for 3DVG is well-motivated and clearly differentiated from prior pinhole-based VLM grounding methods (SeeGround, VLM-Grounder, ZSVG3D); the pinhole-vs-panorama ablation (Tab. 6) provides fairly convincing evidence that 360-degree context specifically helps for queries referencing multiple objects.

Extensive empirical validation: results on ScanRefer, Nr3D, and Sr3D under both single- and multi-dataset training regimes, plus zero-shot comparison against much larger proprietary VLMs, plus two separate generalization studies (unseen scenes via ARKitScenes/3RScan, and unseen text via LLM-generated rephrasings/affordance queries).

The supplementary contains unusually thorough ablations (camera placement scoring factors, adapter layer placement guided by probing analysis, adapter zero-init, TTA rotation count, backbone scalability/efficiency trade-off, and a real-world self-captured deployment test), which substantially strengthens reproducibility and credibility of the design choices.

The training-data construction (deriving 2D box supervision from rendered instance-ID maps) requires no additional manual annotation beyond existing 3D datasets, and the zero-init adapter design is a sensible, well-justified engineering choice.

Strong robustness to underspecified/functional language (+Aff.-N, Mask variants) relative to a competitive supervised baseline (PQ3D), suggesting genuine benefit from VLM-based language reasoning rather than mere lexical matching.
weaknesses: Individual technical components have limited novelty in isolation: the zero-conv adapter is directly borrowed from ControlNet, the EMD digit-loss from an existing LLM-decoding paper, the digit-based bbox decoding scheme from CogVLM, and panoramic rendering/lifting pipelines build heavily on existing NVS/SfM/SAM tools. The contribution is primarily a system-level integration rather than a new algorithmic idea, which should be judged as such but somewhat limits the paper's originality claim.

The pipeline still fundamentally depends on a pre-built, high-quality renderable 3D reconstruction (mesh or 3DGS) with reasonably accurate camera trajectories for the distance-to-trajectory placement term; the paper's framing as relaxing 'high-quality 3D input requirements' relative to traditional point-cloud methods is somewhat overstated, since reconstruction quality (per the 3DGS* ablation, 55.1 vs 61.6 Acc@0.25) clearly still bottlenecks performance.

Efficiency claims are inconsistent: the paper criticizes prior VLM-based methods for being 'computationally prohibitive,' yet the flagship CogVLM-17B configuration itself requires 51.6GB GPU memory and 3.3s per query for a single grounding query, which is not obviously more practical than the criticized proprietary-model baselines for real deployment.

The floor-based, single-level grid assumption for structure-aware camera placement (RANSAC floor + 2D grid) may not generalize to multi-story, sloped, or highly irregular layouts; this is acknowledged only briefly as future work.

The 'two-stage variant' used for ReferIt3D/generalization experiments (matching predicted 2D boxes to GT 3D instance masks via projected IoU) is only lightly described in the main paper, and its potential sensitivity to segmentation/projection noise or ties in matching is not analyzed, despite being central to how the ReferIt3D numbers in Table 1 are obtained.

Performance gains over the strongest existing baselines are sometimes modest (e.g., Sr3D overall 79.1/79.9 vs. UniVLG's 81.7, where PanoGrounder is not best), so the 'state-of-the-art' framing in the abstract/intro is only partially accurate across all benchmarks and splits.

Real-world deployment validation is limited to a single self-captured living-room scene with two qualitative queries, which is insufficient to substantiate the broader practical-deployability claims made in the paper.

strengths: Well-motivated central idea: using 360° panoramic renderings as an intermediate 2D-3D interface addresses a clear limitation (narrow FoV) of prior VLM-based 3DVG methods relying on pinhole images; the panorama-vs-pinhole ablation (Table 6) convincingly demonstrates this benefit, especially for queries mentioning multiple objects.

Strong and consistent empirical results: state-of-the-art or near state-of-the-art performance on ScanRefer, Nr3D, and Sr3D under both single-dataset and multi-dataset training regimes, with particularly large gains on the human-annotated, relation-heavy Nr3D benchmark.

Thorough generalization analysis: cross-dataset evaluation on unseen ARKitScenes and 3RScan scenes, plus systematic text-perturbation experiments (paraphrase, affordance-based, noun-masked queries) showing PanoGrounder is notably more robust than supervised baselines when explicit class cues are removed.

Efficient zero-shot performance: without fine-tuning, PanoGrounder with a comparatively small CogVLM-17B backbone outperforms zero-shot methods built on much larger models (GPT-4V, Qwen2-VL-72B), supporting the claim that the panoramic representation itself (not just backbone scale) drives gains.

Extensive and well-designed ablations, including camera-placement scoring factors with intuitive visual analysis, adapter layer-placement justified via a probing study of the frozen ViT's depth/semantic representations, zero-initialization adapter design, and EMD loss contribution.

Practical validation beyond curated benchmarks: an end-to-end deployment on a casually captured (iPhone video + COLMAP + 3DGS) real scene with runtime/memory breakdown demonstrates feasibility outside lab-clean 3D reconstructions.

Reasonably clear methodological description with well-motivated design choices (zero-conv adapters, visibility-aware cross-view aggregation, EMD digit-level loss) and transparent limitations/future-work discussion.
weaknesses: The pipeline depends on a pre-built renderable 3D reconstruction (mesh or 3DGS); while the paper shows some robustness to automated reconstruction, degraded/incomplete geometry (as shown in the 3DGS artifact examples) still measurably hurts performance, limiting applicability to noisy real-world captures.

Computational cost with the default CogVLM-17B backbone is substantial (multiple forward passes per query due to multi-view aggregation and test-time rotation augmentation, ~3.3s/query, >50GB GPU memory), and while smaller backbones are tested, they trade off meaningful accuracy, so the practical efficiency advantage over prior VLM-based methods is more nuanced than the abstract implies.

Discretized digit-token bounding box regression (999-level quantization) is a coarse localization scheme; the paper does not analyze quantization error or compare against continuous regression alternatives.

The floor-based camera placement (RANSAC single-plane estimation) is tailored to single-story, roughly planar indoor scenes; the authors acknowledge but do not empirically validate the stated future extension to building-level or non-flat/outdoor settings.

Some baseline comparisons in the generalization and cross-dataset tables are re-run by the authors themselves rather than using official released numbers, which, while transparently disclosed, introduces some risk of implementation-dependent bias in comparative claims.

The two-stage variant needed for candidate-box benchmarks (ReferIt3D) is deferred entirely to supplementary material, making it harder to fully assess whether the core panoramic-VLM approach behaves consistently across the proposal-free and proposal-based evaluation settings from the main text alone.
